---
title: "Plotting networks and results"
description: >
  A gallery of the plot methods: networks, matrices, centrality, partitions,
  cores, ego networks, degree and component distributions, the triad census,
  blockmodels, multidimensional scaling, QAP diagnostics, robustness curves,
  and temporal networks, all in base graphics.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
                      fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center")
```

Every result in knappnet that is worth looking at has a plot. The plots use
base graphics only, so they work wherever R does and compose with `par()`,
`layout()`, and the usual devices; every function accepts `...` for the
underlying graphics call (`main`, `xlab`, colors) and returns its input or
the data it drew, invisibly, so a plot can sit in the middle of a pipeline.
Colors follow one scheme across every plot: the color-blind-safe palette
of Okabe and Ito (2008) for categories (eight hues; beyond that the HCL
`"Dark 3"` palette of Zeileis et al. 2020), viridis for numeric scores, and
the single-hue `"Blues 3"` palette for matrices, so a category or a score
looks the same from one plot to the next.

```{r setup}
library(knappnet)
karate <- example_network("karate")
florentine <- example_network("florentine")
```

## Networks

`plot()` on a netframe draws it with a stress layout, nodes sized by degree,
and labels when the network is small. Appearance comes from columns of the
node and edge tables; see `?plot.netframe`.

```{r network}
plot(karate, node_color = "faction", seed = 1, main = "Zachary's karate club")
```

Two helpers wrap the common cases. `plot_centrality()` sizes and colors
nodes by a score and names the legend after it; `plot_partition()` colors
nodes by a grouping and reports its modularity when the grouping carries
one.

```{r overlays}
plot_centrality(karate, betweenness(karate), title = "betweenness", seed = 1)
plot_partition(karate, cluster_louvain(karate, seed = 1), title = "community", seed = 1)
```

`plot_scores()` is the companion ranked dot plot, which answers "who is
highest, and by how much" more precisely than node sizes can.

```{r scores, fig.height = 4}
plot_scores(betweenness(florentine), florentine, main = "Betweenness, Florentine families")
```

## Matrices

Network texts present structure as a permuted adjacency matrix as often as
a drawing. `plot_matrix()` draws the adjacency matrix (or the incidence
matrix of a two-mode network) and, given a partition, sorts the nodes by
group and marks the boundaries.

```{r matrix, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
plot_matrix(karate, order = cluster_louvain(karate, seed = 1), main = "Sorted by community")
```

A `blockmodel()` has both views at once: the permuted matrix and the block
densities, with the 1-blocks of the image outlined.

```{r blockmodel, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
bm <- blockmodel(florentine, concor(florentine, depth = 2))
plot(bm, network = florentine)
```

`plot_mixing_matrix()` shows ties between categories, the raw material of
assortativity and the E-I index.

```{r mixing, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
plot_mixing_matrix(karate, "faction", main = "Ties within and between factions")
assortativity_nominal(karate, "faction")
```

## Distributions and censuses

```{r degree, fig.height = 4}
plot_degree_distribution(karate)
plot_degree_distribution(karate, type = "ccdf", log = TRUE)
```

```{r components, fig.height = 4}
friends <- example_network("noordin", relation = "friendship")
plot_component_sizes(friends)
```

The triad census is drawn against the counts expected under Holland and
Leinhardt's U|MAN null model, which conditions on the dyad census, so the
comparison isolates triadic structure from density and reciprocity.

```{r triads, fig.height = 4.5}
advice <- netframe(data.frame(from = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 1, 2),
                              to   = c(2, 3, 1, 4, 5, 3, 6, 4, 6, 1)))
plot_triad_census(advice, threads = 2)
```

## Cores, ego networks, and robustness

```{r cores, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
plot_coreness(karate, seed = 1, threads = 2, main = "k-core shells")
```

```{r ego}
plot_ego(florentine, "Medici", seed = 1, main = "The Medici and their neighbours")
```

`plot_robustness()` removes nodes in order and tracks the largest component
or the fragmentation, so a chosen set (the key players, say) can be compared
with removal by degree, by betweenness, and at random.

```{r robustness, fig.height = 4.5}
ji <- example_network("jemaah_islamiyah")
kp <- key_players(ji, 3, "fragmentation", seed = 1, threads = 2)
kp$set
plot_robustness(ji, nodes = kp$set, label = "key players", seed = 1, threads = 2)
```

## Scaling

`classical_mds()` results plot as a configuration, a Shepard diagram, or a
scree plot of the eigenvalues.

```{r mds, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
d <- mds_distances(florentine)
fit <- classical_mds(d, k = 2)
fit
plot(fit, main = "Geodesic distances, metric scaling")
```

```{r shepard, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit, which = "shepard", d = d)
```

## Statistical diagnostics

A QAP correlation test plots its permutation distribution with the observed
statistic; an MRQAP plots each coefficient against the interval of its
permutation distribution, or the distributions themselves.

```{r qap, fig.height = 4.5}
set.seed(1)
m <- as.matrix(florentine)
noise <- matrix(rbinom(length(m), 1, 0.15), nrow(m))
noisy <- pmax(m, (noise + t(noise)) > 0)
q <- qap_cor(m, noisy, mode = "graph", reps = 1000, seed = 1, threads = 2)
plot(q)
```

```{r mrqap, fig.height = 4}
set.seed(2)
x1 <- matrix(rnorm(144), 12)
x2 <- matrix(rnorm(144), 12)
y <- 0.8 * x1 + matrix(rnorm(144), 12)
fit <- mrqap(y, list(same = x1, other = x2), reps = 1000, seed = 1, threads = 2)
plot(fit)
plot(fit, which = "distributions")
```

## Temporal networks

`plot_timeline()` shows the raw contact sequence, one row per pair or per
node; `plot_rolling()` draws any measure computed over windows by
`rolling()`.

```{r temporal, fig.height = 4}
logins <- data.frame(user = c("u1", "u2", "u1", "u3", "u2", "u3", "u1", "u2"),
                     host = c("h1", "h1", "h2", "h2", "h3", "h1", "h1", "h2"),
                     time = c(0, 1, 5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 15))
g <- temporal_network(logins)
plot_timeline(g, main = "Logins")
plot_rolling(rolling(g, degree, width = 6, step = 3), main = "Degree in sliding windows")
```

## Spatial networks

Networks with node locations are drawn as maps by `plot_spatial()`, which
`plot()` calls automatically for them; see the article on spatial networks.
